linop

matrix-free linear operators

linop represents a linear operator by the function that applies it, such as a finite-difference stencil, a convolution or a projection, instead of by the matrix of its entries.

You give linop() a function that applies the operator to a block of columns, and the function that applies its conjugate transpose. The object that comes back behaves like a matrix under %*%, t(), crossprod(), + and *. Each of these operations adds a node to an expression graph, so nothing is computed until you apply the result to a vector or a block. An operator also carries capabilities, such as being Hermitian or positive definite, each with a record of the argument that established it, so you can see what a claim rests on and decide what a solver may rely on. linop supports:

  • Operators too large to store. A 262,144 x 262,144 image blur, 512 GiB as a dense matrix, is applied in 0.0095 seconds with a peak memory of 51 MB (details).
  • Solving systems and computing spectra. solve() chooses among seven Krylov methods on the operator’s declared capabilities and shape, and eigs() and svds() compute eigenpairs and singular triplets. Each result carries a certificate.
  • Capabilities with their evidence. Properties propagate through the algebra together with the argument behind them, and a solver states the evidence it accepts as a requirement().
  • Checking a hand-written operator. verify() runs the contract every solver relies on, including the adjoint consistency test that catches a wrong conjugation.
  • Operators on infinite index sets. A dimension may be Inf: linop_jacobi() builds a self-adjoint operator on the sequence space l^2(Z), and eigs() runs on the operator itself.

Every solver is checked against closed-form truth. The propagation rules for capabilities are checked by 9,892 brute-force soundness checks against materialised matrices.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/linop")

Usage

  1. Build an operator with linop() from a function and its adjoint, or from a matrix you already hold.
  2. Combine operators with ordinary matrix arithmetic. The result is a lazy expression.
  3. Apply it with %*%, or pass it to solve(), eigs() or svds().
  4. Check a hand-written operator with verify().

The smallest operator is two functions and a shape. S shifts a vector up by one position and pads with a zero; its conjugate transpose shifts down:

library(linop)

n <- 8
up <- function(X) rbind(X[-1, , drop = FALSE], 0)
down <- function(X) rbind(0, X[-n, , drop = FALSE])
S <- linop(up, adjoint = down, dim = c(n, n))

S %*% 1:8
#> [1] 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 0

The function receives a block of columns, so a matrix goes through one column at a time and a vector comes back as a vector, as with a matrix.

Arithmetic on operators builds an expression. The tree printed below is the expression as written; nothing has been applied or allocated:

B <- crossprod(S) + 0.1 * linop_eye(n)
B
#> <linop> 8 x 8, double
#>   hermitian, symmetric, positive_semidefinite, real
#> 
#> sum
#> |- product
#> |  |- transpose
#> |  |  `- fun[8 x 8]
#> |  `- fun[8 x 8]
#> `- scale by 0.1
#>    `- I[8]

Applying B walks the tree right to left, one block at a time. A linear system in B is solved with R’s own solve(), which returns the solution with a certificate attached:

rhs <- as.numeric(B %*% rep(1, n))
x <- solve(B, rhs)
round(as.numeric(x), 10)
#> [1] 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1

Getting started with linop builds operators from matrices and sparse matrices, and covers the transpose, adjoint and conjugate views and complex operators.

Operators too large to store

A 512 x 512 image blur is written as the function that blurs one column and reused as its own adjoint:

side <- 512L
n_img <- side * side

shift_up <- function(M) rbind(M[-1, , drop = FALSE], M[side, , drop = FALSE])
shift_down <- function(M) rbind(M[1, , drop = FALSE], M[-side, , drop = FALSE])

smooth <- function(v) {
  M <- matrix(v, side, side)
  M <- (M + shift_up(M) + shift_down(M)) / 3
  M <- t(M)
  M <- (M + shift_up(M) + shift_down(M)) / 3
  as.vector(t(M))
}

blur <- function(X) {
  Y <- X
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(X))) Y[, j] <- smooth(X[, j])
  Y
}

sym <- c(symmetric = TRUE, hermitian = TRUE)
Blur <- linop(blur, adjoint = blur, dim = c(n_img, n_img),
               properties = sym)

Blur is 262,144 x 262,144, which is 512 GiB written out as doubles. The Tikhonov normal-equations operator for deblurring the image is one line:

N <- crossprod(Blur) + 1e-3 * linop_eye(n_img)
img <- runif(n_img)
y <- N %*% img
Operator 262,144 x 262,144
Dense storage for the same operator 512 GiB
One apply of Blur 0.0095 s
One apply of crossprod(Blur) + 1e-3 * I 0.019 s
Peak R memory across the run 51 MB

The timings were taken with R 4.6.0 on Windows 11, an i9-14900K and the reference BLAS. The expression is applied one block at a time, so the memory figure is set by the block you hand it and by the operator’s own working set. Wrapping a callback costs 200 ns per apply, which is 0.13% or less of one application of an operator with 1e5 elements or more.

The expression graph covers the simplification rules, the cost model, collapse() and materialisation.

Capabilities and their evidence

An operator records what is known about it together with the argument that established it, and both travel through the algebra. adjoint(A) %*% A is Hermitian whatever is claimed about A, so the product node records it from its construction:

A <- linop(matrix(c(2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 1, 0, 1, 2), 3, 3))
G <- adjoint(A) %*% A
cap(G, "hermitian")
#> TRUE  (construction / identity / conf 1)

When two operators are declared positive definite by their author, their sum is positive definite by a sound rule, and the declarations it rests on stay visible underneath:

id <- function(X) X
twice <- function(X) 2 * X
pd <- c(hermitian = TRUE, positive_definite = TRUE)
P <- linop(id, adjoint = id, dim = c(4, 4), properties = pd)
Q <- linop(twice, adjoint = twice, dim = c(4, 4), properties = pd)

cap(P + Q, "positive_definite")
#> TRUE  (construction / identity / conf 1 <- [user_declaration / identity / conf 1; user_declaration / identity / conf 1])

A solver states what it accepts as a predicate over the whole chain. This one accepts construction, computation and theorems, and refuses a chain that ends in a user’s declaration:

req <- requirement(sources = c("construction", "computation", "theorem"))
evidence_satisfies(cap(P + Q, "positive_definite")$evidence, req)
#> [1] FALSE

Values are three-valued. NA means unknown and is never read as FALSE, and a propagation rule that cannot prove TRUE returns NA. Capabilities and evidence lists the capabilities and the rules that propagate them.

Checking an operator

verify() runs the contract that every solver in the package relies on, and reports each check with its own status:

verify(S)
#> check                          status       source           guarantee             conf
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> adjoint consistency            pass         computation      identity              1
#> view identities                pass         computation      identity              1
#> real transpose equals adjoint  pass         computation      identity              1
#> linearity                      pass         computation      identity              1
#> block consistency              pass         computation      identity              1
#> shape and dtype                pass         computation      identity              1
#> complex linearity              pass         computation      identity              1
#> declared capabilities          not_checked  probe            heuristic             -
#> purity                         pass         computation      identity              1
#> gemm agreement                 pass         computation      identity              1
#> materialisation agreement      pass         computation      identity              1
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> overall                        qualified   no deterministic bound on: declared capabilities

The certificate keeps the checks that carry no deterministic bound in a list of their own. A wrong conjugation in an adjoint is the most common bug in a hand-written operator, and the adjoint consistency check fails on it. Here the adjoint is a copy of the forward action:

Bad <- linop(up, adjoint = up, dim = c(n, n))
verify(Bad)$overall
#> [1] "fail"

An adapter for another storage format is one linop() method for its class, followed by verify() on an instance. Writing an adapter shows it, with node registration and the preconditioner contract.

Solvers and eigensolvers

solve() reaches seven Krylov methods for linear systems, and enforces the preconditioner contract in each method that accepts a preconditioner. eigs() is a Hermitian eigensolver and svds() a singular value solver. Each result carries a certificate, read with certificate(), with the operator-norm estimate its arithmetic floor rests on.

eigs() and svds() have two engines. The reference engine in this package is a restarted Lanczos iteration with full reorthogonalisation, which holds its whole basis in each round. The PRIMME library restarts implicitly and keeps a basis of fixed small size; it is available when the companion package linop.primme is installed, and the default method = "auto" then takes it. Whichever engine runs, the reported values are measured on the operator and the certificate is the same object, with a record of which engine ran and why.

Solving a system, Eigenvalues and singular values and Reading a certificate cover each verb and what comes back.

Operators on a sequence space

A dimension may be Inf. linop_jacobi() builds a self-adjoint operator on l^2(Z) whose essential spectrum is exact by Weyl’s theorem and whose eigenvectors decay at a closed-form rate, and finite_section() truncates it. eigs() runs on the operator itself and chooses the truncation width: outside the window the tail is exactly geometric, so the width that meets a tolerance is a division. The certificate that comes back is a statement about the operator on l^2(Z) itself. Operators on a sequence space works through an example.

Related packages

  • eigencore provides matrix-free block eigensolvers with an as_operator() adapter generic, complex dense arithmetic, block Krylov methods, shift-invert and certificates, through a constructor-object interface.
  • Matrix provides stored sparse and structured matrix classes with direct factorisations for them.
  • sanic provides direct and Krylov solvers for sparse linear systems.
  • amatrix provides backend-agnostic stored matrix classes, including GPU backends.
